content.title: The Islamic Ruling on Eating Puja Food and Prasad
content.subtitle: Preserving Faith over Compromise: Avoiding Shirk in Social Harmony
content.body:
During Durga Puja and Lakshmi Puja, neighbors, colleagues, and acquaintances often offer sweets, naru, batasha, or fruits. Sometimes, out of social courtesy, embarrassment, or fear of damaging relationships, people accept and eat them. But have we ever considered that consuming food offered with the intention of pleasing a created being is not merely about eating—it may put our Tawheed at serious risk? Social courtesy is important in a Muslim’s life, but when it crosses the clear boundaries set by the Lord of the heavens and the earth, it can have grave consequences for a believer.

The Qur’an’s Clear Declaration and Prohibition

Islam has strict principles regarding the consumption of lawful and pure food. The Qur’an explicitly declares forbidden the food dedicated to an idol, deity, or anyone besides Allah for their pleasure:

“He has only forbidden you carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that which has been dedicated to anyone other than Allah...” (Surah Al-Baqarah, 2:173)

Puja prasad is not merely a sweet or ordinary food; it is presented as an offering before deities and dedicated for their pleasure. Consuming such food directly contradicts this clear Qur’anic command.

The Position of the Companions and Guidance from Islamic Jurisprudence

Clear guidance regarding food dedicated to anyone besides Allah has existed since the time of the Companions and their successors. When Mother Aishah (RA) was asked about the festival food of fire-worshippers and polytheists, she advised avoiding the meat of animals they slaughtered and food dedicated to their idols [Musannaf Ibn Abi Shaybah: 24722]. According to the consensus of the four schools of Islamic jurisprudence, including the Hanafi school, consuming food offered in worship or prasad is impermissible and haram for Muslims [Al-Bahr ar-Ra’iq: 8/555].

Gifts vs. Prasad: Understanding the Subtle Difference

A common question is whether Muslims can ever accept food from non-Muslim neighbors. Here, an important distinction must be understood. Islam does not prohibit accepting ordinary gifts, fruits, or otherwise halal food from non-Muslim neighbors when they are not part of a religious ritual. However, accepting food placed on an altar as part of their worship or distributed as prasad is tantamount to endorsing their religious act of shirk.

Social Etiquette and a Respectful Refusal

It is possible to maintain the boundaries of faith without offending non-Muslim colleagues or neighbors. When someone offers prasad, respond politely rather than harshly: “Thank you for your kindness, but according to our religious beliefs and Islamic law, we are not permitted to eat prasad or food offered as part of a religious ritual.” Upholding your convictions with dignity does not diminish your standing in the eyes of people of other faiths; rather, it can earn respect for you as a principled Muslim.

It is never wise to consume something that may extinguish the light within our hearts and invite our Lord’s displeasure simply to maintain worldly relationships or out of momentary hesitation. Let us maintain kindness, good citizenship, and human compassion toward non-Muslims while making no compromise on the purity of our food or the principles of Tawheed.

(Note: These recommendations are based on the guidance of knowledgeable scholars and are intended to safeguard the spiritual well-being of Muslims. They are not meant to demean anyone or hurt anyone’s religious sentiments.)
